meta.description: Not Bob Marley — these are Robert Neville’s lines in the 2007 film I Am Legend, written by Mark Protosevich and Akiva Goldsman. No Marley source exists.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The people who are trying to make this world worse are not taking a day off. How can I? Light up the darkness'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Bob Marley. It’s scripted movie dialogue from I Am Legend (2007) — Wikiquote files it under Misattributed. Here’s the real origin.

answer.label: Not Bob Marley — a line from the film ‘I Am Legend’
answer.authorDates: Written for “I Am Legend” · released 2007 · Warner Bros.
answer.sourceLine: These exact words are spoken by Robert Neville (Will Smith) in the 2007 film “I Am Legend,” where he retells a Bob Marley anecdote. Wikiquote files the line under “Misattributed”, noting there is no indication Marley ever spoke them; the phrasing — especially “Light up the darkness” — is scripted movie dialogue by writers Mark Protosevich and Akiva Goldsman.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Robert Neville (Will Smith), retelling a Bob Marley story

source.excerpt: He believed that you could cure racism and hate… literally cure it, by injecting music and love into people’s lives. When he was scheduled to perform at a peace rally, a gunman came to his house and shot him down. Two days later he walked out on that stage and sang. When they asked him why, he said, “The people who are trying to make this world worse are not taking a day off. How can I? Light up the darkness.”
trail: Wikiquote lists this exact line under “Misattributed,” stating it originated in the 2007 film “I Am Legend” and that there is no indication the words were spoken by Marley.
Wikiquote’s I Am Legend page reproduces the identical wording as Robert Neville’s dialogue, crediting writers Mark Protosevich and Akiva Goldsman.

The film’s framing draws on a real episode: Marley was shot at 56 Hope Road on 3 December 1976 yet performed a 90-minute set at the Smile Jamaica Concert on 5 December 1976 — but no documented Marley statement matches these words.
The misattribution spread widely after director Taika Waititi shared the line as Marley’s in March 2019, as noted on Wikiquote.
source.excerptNote: Robert Neville’s dialogue in “I Am Legend” (2007). The framing story is loosely inspired by a real event — Marley was shot on 3 December 1976 and still performed at the Smile Jamaica Concert two days later — but the quoted words themselves are the screenwriters’.
source.rightsHolder: Warner Bros. Entertainment (screenwriters Mark Protosevich & Akiva Goldsman)
source.rightsNote: The wording first appears as scripted dialogue in Warner Bros.’ 2007 film “I Am Legend,” so the line is in copyright as part of that screenplay. It is not a Bob Marley quotation and has no public-domain status.

author.name: Mark Protosevich & Akiva Goldsman
author.heading: Who actually wrote the line
author.metaLine: Screenwriters of I Am Legend (2007) · dir. Francis Lawrence · Warner Bros.
author.bio: Mark Protosevich and Akiva Goldsman wrote the screenplay for the 2007 sci-fi film I Am Legend, directed by Francis Lawrence and starring Will Smith. The “make this world worse… light up the darkness” speech is delivered by Smith’s character, Robert Neville, as a piece of in-story dialogue about Bob Marley — not a documented Marley quotation. Goldsman is an Academy Award–winning screenwriter (A Beautiful Mind).

misattribution.heading: How a movie line became a “Bob Marley quote”
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most widely circulated fake Bob Marley quotes online — and its origin is unusually easy to pin down. The words were written for a Hollywood film.

items.why: The line is spoken by Robert Neville (Will Smith) in the 2007 film “I Am Legend,” retelling a Marley story. Wikiquote places it in its Misattributed section, noting “there is no indication that the quoted words were actually spoken by Bob Marley.” No interview, recording, or transcript documents Marley saying this — and “Light up the darkness” is a screenwriters’ flourish, not his phrasing.

items.who: Taika Waititi (as a spreader, not originator)
items.why: The filmmaker publicly shared the line as Marley’s in March 2019, an instance recorded on Wikiquote that helped push the movie dialogue further into circulation as a genuine quote.

misattribution.truthLine: The words were written by Mark Protosevich and Akiva Goldsman for Robert Neville’s dialogue in “I Am Legend” (2007) — a fictional retelling, not a Bob Marley quotation.

context.heading: The real event behind the fiction
lead: The film’s anecdote is loosely rooted in fact. On 3 December 1976, gunmen stormed Bob Marley’s home at 56 Hope Road in Kingston and wounded him, his wife Rita, and manager Don Taylor, days before a free concert amid Jamaica’s violent election season. Two days later, Marley still performed a roughly 90-minute set at the Smile Jamaica Concert on 5 December, at one point baring his wounded arm and telling the crowd “Bang bang, I’m OK.”

That courage is real and documented. What is not documented is the specific, tidy quotation the internet attaches to it. The screenwriters distilled the spirit of the moment into a memorable line for Will Smith’s character — and the line later escaped the movie and got pinned on Marley himself.
detailsBody: Marley went into brief hiding after the shooting and left Jamaica soon after, recording much of the album “Exodus” abroad in 1977.
Because the words are catalogued as misattributed rather than tied to any Marley text, they carry no public-domain status — the phrasing belongs to a 2007 screenplay.
context.pull: The courage was real. The quotation is a screenwriter’s line.
